clinicalPearls: A complication of chronically poorly controlled, insulin-deficient type 1 diabetes mellitus, described historically in children and adolescents.
Classic constellation of growth failure with short stature, tender hepatomegaly from hepatic glycogen loading (glycogenic hepatopathy), a cushingoid habitus and delayed puberty.
Glycogenic hepatopathy is the hepatic hallmark — reversible glycogen overloading of hepatocytes that is distinct from non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
Transaminases may be strikingly raised yet typically normalise once stable glycaemic control is restored.
Wide swings between hyperglycaemia and periods of insulin excess drive the hepatic glycogen accumulation.
Growth retardation is linked to disruption of the growth hormone–IGF-1 axis with hepatic growth hormone resistance despite adequate or high growth hormone.
Now uncommon where modern insulin regimens are available, but still seen with poor adherence, insulin omission or limited access to care.
The disorder is largely reversible, underscoring the value of restoring consistent glycaemic control.
reference.pathophysiology: Mauriac syndrome arises in the setting of chronic insulin deficiency with erratic glycaemic control, classically in a child or adolescent with type 1 diabetes who oscillates between prolonged hyperglycaemia and episodes of insulin excess. Fluctuating glucose and insulin availability drive excessive hepatic uptake and storage of glucose as glycogen, producing the reversible glycogen overloading of hepatocytes known as glycogenic hepatopathy, which manifests as tender hepatomegaly and often striking transaminase elevation. Persistent metabolic derangement disturbs the growth hormone–IGF-1 axis, with hepatic growth hormone resistance and low IGF-1 despite adequate or elevated growth hormone, explaining the growth failure and delayed puberty, while counter-regulatory cortisol excess and altered fat distribution contribute the cushingoid habitus. Because the underlying lesion is functional rather than structural, restoration of stable glycaemic control typically reverses the hepatic, growth and pubertal abnormalities.
additionalDifferentials: Hepatic glycogen storage disorders (e.g. glycogen storage disease type I)
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and steatohepatitis
Coeliac disease as a cause of growth failure in type 1 diabetes
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
additionalInvestigations: Glycated haemoglobin and review of continuous or capillary glucose monitoring data
Liver function tests with serial transaminases to demonstrate reversibility
Liver ultrasound to characterise hepatomegaly and hepatic echogenicity
Liver biopsy in diagnostic doubt, with special stains to distinguish glycogen from steatosis
IGF-1, IGFBP-3 and assessment of the growth hormone axis
Bone age radiograph to quantify skeletal maturation
Coeliac and thyroid autoimmunity screening given associated conditions
redFlags: Recurrent diabetic ketoacidosis or severe hypoglycaemia indicating dangerously unstable control
Rapidly enlarging tender liver or marked, unexplained rise in transaminases
Progressive growth arrest with falling height velocity
Clues to insulin omission or a psychosocial crisis underlying poor adherence
reference.prognosis: The syndrome is largely reversible, and hepatomegaly, transaminitis and growth usually improve with sustained, stable glycaemic control. Persistently poor control risks permanent short stature and the accrual of long-term microvascular complications.
pitfalls: Mistaking glycogenic hepatopathy for fatty liver disease, which carries different management and prognosis.
Attributing the transaminitis to unrelated liver disease and overlooking the glycaemic cause.
Over-aggressive insulin correction that worsens hepatic glycogen loading and provokes hypoglycaemia.
Overlooking associated autoimmune conditions such as coeliac disease and hypothyroidism as contributors to growth failure.
management: Restore stable, sustained glycaemic control by optimising the insulin regimen (basal-bolus, insulin pump or continuous glucose monitoring), which reverses the syndrome
Structured diabetes education and adherence support to eliminate the wide swings between hyperglycaemia and insulin excess
Dietetic input and management of the eating and behavioural factors contributing to erratic control
Serial monitoring of liver function to confirm resolution of the glycogenic hepatopathy and transaminitis
Monitor growth, pubertal development and the growth hormone-IGF-1 axis, expecting catch-up with improved control
Screen for and manage emerging microvascular complications of diabetes
Psychosocial and family support, involving a paediatric diabetes multidisciplinary team
